newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope's visits in step with Poland's evolution.
newsitem.headline: Pope's visits in step with Poland's evolution.

text.p: Since Cardinal Karol Wojtyla left his Krakow diocese in 1978 for a Vatican conclave, little dreaming he would become Pope John Paul ll, his visits to his homeland have been landmarks in Poland's evolution.
Here is a list of the Pope's previous trips to Poland and their place in the context of its recent history.
1976 - A round of price increases sparks major protests by workers against the communist authorities.
Oct 16, 1978 - Cardinal Wojtyla is elected the first non-Italian Pope in 455 years. His pontificate begins officially six days later.

June 2-10, 1979 - The Pope returns on a triumphant pilgrimage to communist-ruled Poland, infusing its people with self-confidence which many historians say contributed to the creation of Solidarity, the Soviet bloc's first free trade union. "Let Thy Spirit descend and renew the face of this land," he calls out in prayer.

August 1980 - After a wave of strikes for pay rises and recognition of free unions, the government caves in to workers' key demands. On August 31 in Gdansk, Solidarity leader Lech Walesa signs an agreement using a huge pen bearing the image of the Pope.
December 13, 1981 - General Wojciech Jaruzelski imposes martial law, clamping down on Solidarity and unleashing mass arrests.

June 16-23, 1983 - The Pope makes his second visit to Poland, where martial law had been suspended but not lifted. He is greeted by around 10 million people, sees Walesa privately and meets Jaruzelski, stressing the need for democratic rights.
October 19, 1984 - Pro-Solidarity Catholic priest Father Jerzy Popieluszko murdered by security police agents.

July 8-14, 1987 - The Pope visits Solidarity's strongholds of Solidarity, Gdansk, Gdynia and Szczecin on the Baltic coast. He is greeted by huge crowds waving Solidarity banners and speaks out for trade union rights, repeatedly calling on solidarity as a value, notably at a Mass in Gdansk.
August 1988 - After renewed strikes, Walesa and Interior Minister Czeslaw Kiszczak agree to Round Table talks which will lead to a transfer of power.
February-April 1989 - Round Table talks held.
June 1989 - Semi-free elections held, bringing overwhelming Solidarity triumph.
24 August 1989 - A former dissident, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, becomes prime minister.
December 1990 - Walesa freely elected president of Poland.

June 1-9, 1991 - The Pontiff pays his first to newly democratic Poland. He gives encouragement amid economic hardship and unemployment, but tells Poles to hold to their values amid pressures brought by freedom -- secularisation and materialism. "It is necessary to learn how to be free," he says during homilies in successive cities on the Ten Commandments.
August 13-16, 1991 - The Pope attends a world gathering of youth at the Jasna Gora monastery in southern Poland.
September 1993 - Former communists, now social democrats, emerge as strongest party in elections and form a coalition government.

May 22, 1995 - Pope John Paul, on a brief visit in the South, admonishes Poles for allowing spoils of their post-communist freedom to be eroded by moral decay, expresses worry about the course his country is taking.
November 1995 - Walesa beaten by ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski in presidential elections.

May 31-June 10 - The Pope makes a new visit to Poland as political battles rage between the ex-communists and Solidarity supporters before elections likely in September, partly over religious-related issues, such as abortion and a concordat treaty with the Vatican.
